title: The operator is the part that decides the door
author: Böss Group
excerpt: Most of a shutter specification goes into the slat. The failures that bring an installer back come from the operator — and almost always from one of three decisions made when it was chosen.
body: A shutter specification usually goes into the curtain: slat profile, gauge, finish, perforation. The part that decides how the door behaves for the next decade is the operator.

Three things separate operators, and none of them is price. Capacity, matched to weighed curtain mass rather than opening area. Duty, which is how many cycles a day it will run before heat becomes the limit. And what happens when the power fails — a chain hand-drive, a DC unit that lifts by hand, or a battery back-up sized to the motor.

Three ways to get it wrong, in the order they show up on service calls: buying on price alone; fitting a small operator to a large curtain, which works on the first day and shortens from there; and never servicing it, because an operator that is never inspected fails at the brake rather than at the motor.
Industrial operators add an automatic brake and safety sensing. On a door that runs all day, the brake is the part doing the real work.
